The binomial theorem gives
4n=(1+1)2n=∑k=02n​(k2n​).
(1)
The central binomial coefficient is the largest of these 2n+1 nonnegative binomial coefficients, so
(n2n​)≥2n+14n​=2n+122n​.
(2)
For the upper bound, fix a prime number p≤2n. By Legendre formula,
vp​((n2n​))=∑j≥1​(⌊pj2n​⌋−2⌊pjn​⌋).
(3)
Each summand is either zero or one. Hence the P-adic valuation satisfies
vp​((n2n​))≤⌊logplog(2n)​⌋.
(4)
If p≤2n​, this implies
pvp​((n2n​))≤2n.
(5)
There are at most 2n​ such prime numbers. If instead p>2n​, then p2>2n, so the P-adic valuation is at most one. Multiplying the prime-power contributions therefore yields
(n2n​)≤(2n)2n​∏p≤2np prime​​p.
(6)

Write the Chebyshev theta function as
ϑ(x)=∑p≤xp prime​​logp.
(7)
Taking natural logarithms in part a gives
2nlog2−log(2n+1)≤2n​log(2n)+ϑ(2n),
(8)
and hence
ϑ(2n)≥2nlog2−2n​log(2n)−log(2n+1).
(9)
Because n​logn/n→0, the right-hand side is at least n/2 for every sufficiently large integer n.
Now let x be sufficiently large and set n=⌊x/2⌋ using the floor function. Then 2n≤x and n≥x/3, so the monotonicity of ϑ gives
p≤xp prime​∑​logp=ϑ(x)≥ϑ(2n)≥2n​≥6x​≥12x​.​
(10)

c

Words: 107 Articles: 1
1G OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 107
c OurBigBook.com
Suppose that the positive integer n is a decisive number. For every prime number p<n​, the composite number p2 satisfies 1<p2<n. It therefore cannot be coprime to n, so p∣n.
The product of all prime numbers below n​ consequently divides n. Taking natural logarithms gives
logn≥∑p<n​​logp.
(11)
Changing the strict endpoint can remove at most one prime term. By part b, for every sufficiently large n the right-hand side is at least, for example, n​/13. This is impossible for sufficiently large n, since
lognn​​⟶∞.
(12)
Thus every decisive number lies below one fixed bound, and only finitely many integers can do so.

i OurBigBook.com
The polynomial form of Runge theorem says that if K⊂C is compact, C∖K is connected, and f is holomorphic on a neighbourhood of K, then for every ε>0 there is a polynomial P such that
supz∈K​∣f(z)−P(z)∣<ε.
(13)
Statement (i) is false. Take the entire function f(z)=e−z. It is bounded on the closed first quadrant E. If polynomials Pn​ converged uniformly to f on E, then each sufficiently late Pn​ would be bounded on the positive real axis. A polynomial bounded on that ray must be constant. No sequence of constants converges uniformly to e−x on [0,∞), since its values at zero and near infinity differ by one.
Solved by gpt-5.6-sol high.

ii

Words: 52 Articles: 1
2F OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 52
ii OurBigBook.com
Statement (ii) is true. Let
Kn​=E∩{z:∣z∣≤n}.
(14)
Each Kn​ is compact and has connected complement. By the polynomial Runge theorem, choose a polynomial Pn​ with
supKn​​∣Pn​−f∣<n1​.
(15)
Every fixed z∈E belongs to Kn​ for all sufficiently large n, so Pn​(z)→f(z). Thus the convergence is pointwise on E.
Solved by gpt-5.6-sol high.

Solution

Words: 81
iii OurBigBook.com
Statement (iii) is false. Let Ω be a thin open annulus about the unit circle, let f(z)=1/z, and split the circle into two proper closed arcs K1​,K2​ whose union is the whole circle. Each arc has connected complement, so polynomial approximation of the reciprocal on a proper circular arc gives uniform polynomial approximations to f on each Kj​ separately.
If polynomials Pn​ converged uniformly to 1/z on K1​∪K2​, then uniform convergence on the unit circle and the Cauchy integral theorem would give
0=limn→∞​∫∣z∣=1​Pn​(z)dz=∫∣z∣=1​zdz​=2πi,
(16)
a contradiction.
Solved by gpt-5.6-sol high.

Words: 42 Articles: 1

Solution

Words: 42
iv OurBigBook.com
Statement (iv) is true. Apply the Weierstrass approximation theorem separately to the real and imaginary parts of the continuous function f on the compact interval [0,1]. Combining the two real polynomial sequences gives complex polynomials converging uniformly to f on I.

3I (Coding and Cryptography)

Words: 200 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 200
3I OurBigBook.com
Write 1n​ for the all-one column vector. The parity-check extension of a linear code is
C+={(c1​,…,cn​,c1​+⋯+cn​):c∈C}.
(17)
The defining map C→F2n+1​ is linear, so C+ is a binary linear code. If G is a generator matrix and H a parity-check matrix for C, then one may take
G+=(G​G1n​​),H+=(H1nT​​01​).
(18)
The punctured code in, say, the last coordinate is
C−={(c1​,…,cn−1​):c∈C}.
(19)
Coordinate deletion is a linear map, so C− is linear. Its generator matrix G− is obtained by deleting the last column of G. If the minimum distance is at least two, deletion is injective on C, and hence C− has the same dimension as C.
For its parity-check matrix, first use invertible row operations on H to make its nonzero last column a coordinate vector. The last column is nonzero because otherwise the weight-one word supported there would belong to C, contrary to d≥2. Delete the pivot row and the last column; the resulting matrix H− is a parity-check matrix for C−. Equivalently, (C−)⊥ is obtained by shortening the dual code C⊥ at the deleted coordinate.
Finally, the shortened code in the last coordinate is
C′={(c1​,…,cn−1​):(c1​,…,cn−1​,0)∈C}.
(20)
It is linear whenever C is linear, because it is the puncture of the subspace C∩{xn​=0}.
Solved by gpt-5.6-sol high.

ii OurBigBook.com
The grammars are non-equivalent. In the first grammar, terminal derivations without AB→c give
{arbs:r,s≥1}.
(25)
After applying B→Bb any number of times while A and B remain adjacent, the production AB→c also gives
{cbt:t≥0}.
(26)
Hence, in particular, ab∈L(G0​) and c∈L(G0​).
In the second grammar, the fixed terminals ab in XabY prevent X and Y from ever becoming adjacent, so XY→c can never be used. The remaining productions give exactly
L(G1​)={arbs:r,s≥2}.
(27)
Thus ab,c∈/L(G1​), proving that the generated languages differ.

iii

Solution
Words: 82
iii OurBigBook.com
The first grammar generates
L(G0​)={ab2r+1a:r≥0},
(28)
because A→bAb adds two b's and A→b terminates the derivation.
In the second grammar, Z is a nonproductive nonterminal: every right-hand side of a Z-production still contains a Z. Consequently the branch Y→ZZ never yields a terminal word. Every terminal derivation from Y instead uses Y→bYb repeatedly and ends with Y→b, so
L(G1​)={ab2r+1a:r≥0}=L(G0​).
(29)
The grammars are therefore equivalent, although they are not isomorphic.

Words: 92
5J OurBigBook.com
A one-parameter exponential family with natural statistic Y has density or probability mass function
fθ​(y)=h(y)exp{θy−K(θ)},
(30)
where θ is the natural parameter of an exponential family and K is the cumulant function of an exponential family. Its mean parameter is
μ(θ)=K′(θ).
(31)
The exponential-family deviance from θ1​ to θ2​ is twice the Kullback-Leibler divergence:
D(θ1​,θ2​)=2Eθ1​​[logfθ2​​(Y)fθ1​​(Y)​].
(32)
The carrier h(Y) cancels from the likelihood ratio, so, with μ1​=Eθ1​​Y,
D(θ1​,θ2​)=2{(θ1​−θ2​)μ1​−K(θ1​)+K(θ2​)}.​
(33)
For the Poisson distribution with mean μ,
θ=logμ,K(θ)=eθ=μ.
(34)
Therefore
D(μ1​,μ2​)=2{μ1​logμ2​μ1​​−μ1​+μ2​}.​
(35)
Writing μ2​=μ1​+δ and applying the Taylor series of log(1+δ/μ1​) gives
D(μ1​,μ1​+δ)=μ1​δ2​+O(δ3),
(36)
so the second-order approximation is
D(μ1​,μ2​)≃μ1​(μ2​−μ1​)2​.​
(37)

6C OurBigBook.com
With s=0, the equilibria satisfy
g(1+g2kg​−1)=0.
(38)
Besides g=0, the two positive equilibria are
g±​=2k±k2−4​​,g−​<1<g+​,
(39)
where g−​g+​=1. Since
∂g​f(g,0)=(1+g2)22kg​−1,
(40)
the nonzero equilibrium relation k=(1+g2)/g gives
∂g​f(g,0)=1+g21−g2​.
(41)
The fixed point stability for an autonomous differential equation therefore shows that g=0 and g+​ are stable, while g−​ is unstable. The graph of f(g,0) starts at zero with negative slope, crosses upward at g−​, crosses downward at g+​, and tends to −∞ as g→∞.
For a constant input s, write the equilibrium equation as
s=h(g),h(g)=g−1+g2kg2​.
(42)
The low stable equilibrium and the intervening unstable equilibrium coalesce in a saddle-node bifurcation. More precisely, let gc​ be the first positive solution of
h′(gc​)=1−(1+gc2​)22kgc​​=0
(43)
and define
sc​(k)=h(gc​)=gc​−1+gc2​kgc2​​.​
(44)
Equivalently, f(gc​,sc​)=0 and ∂g​f(gc​,sc​)=0, with gc​ on the low-concentration branch. If s1​>sc​(k), that branch no longer exists. Holding the input long enough carries the trajectory into the basin of attraction of the high state. When the input returns to zero, the concentration converges to
g∗=g+​=2k+k2−4​​.​
(45)
This is the saturating autocatalytic switch.
For k≫1, the threshold occurs at g=O(k−1), so
f(g,s)=s+kg2−g+O(kg4).
(46)
The approximate double-root conditions are
s+kg2−g=0,2kg−1=0.
(47)
Thus gc​≃1/(2k) and
sc​(k)≃4k1​.​
(48)
Hence the constant in sc​(k)≃Ck−1 is C=1/4​, as recorded by the strong-autocatalysis switching threshold.

Words: 199
7E OurBigBook.com
For
w′′+p(z)w′+q(z)w=0,
(49)
a finite point z0​ is an ordinary point exactly when p and q are holomorphic there. It is a regular singular point exactly when
(z−z0​)p(z)and(z−z0​)2q(z)
(50)
are holomorphic at z0​.
Put ζ=1/z and W(ζ)=w(1/ζ). Direct differentiation gives
w′=−ζ2W′,w′′=ζ4W′′+2ζ3W′,
(51)
so the transformed equation is
W′′+(ζ2​−ζ2p(1/ζ)​)W′+ζ4q(1/ζ)​W=0.
(52)
Consequently z=∞ is ordinary precisely when
ζ2​−ζ2p(1/ζ)​andζ4q(1/ζ)​
(53)
are holomorphic at ζ=0. It is a regular singular point at infinity precisely when zp(z) and z2q(z) are holomorphic functions of 1/z near infinity.
If zero and infinity are regular singular and every nonzero finite point is ordinary, the Laurent series of p and q can contain only the terms compatible with both endpoint bounds. Hence
p(z)=za​,q(z)=z2b​​
(54)
for constants a,b. The equation is a Cauchy-Euler differential equation. Its indicial equation is
λ(λ−1)+aλ+b=0.
(55)
For distinct roots λ1​,λ2​, the general solution on a domain with a chosen logarithm branch is
w(z)=C1​zλ1​+C2​zλ2​.
(56)
For a repeated root λ, the general solution of an Euler-Cauchy equation is
w(z)=zλ(C1​+C2​logz).
(57)
Finally require infinity to be ordinary. In the transformed equation its coefficients become
ζ2−a​,ζ2b​.
(58)
Both are holomorphic at zero exactly when a=2 and b=0. Thus the further restriction is
p(z)=z2​,q(z)=0.​
(59)

∂pi​∂D​=qi​,∂qi​∂D​=pi​.

q⋅∇q​f−p⋅∇p​f=0.​

The uniformization theorem states that every simply connected Riemann surface is conformally equivalent to exactly one of the Riemann sphere C∞​, the complex plane C, or the open unit disc D. Equivalently, every connected Riemann surface is a quotient of one of these by a free properly discontinuous group of conformal automorphisms.
For C∞​, every nonidentity Möbius transformation has a fixed point. A free action is therefore trivial, so the only surface uniformized by the sphere is
C∞​.​
(220)
Every conformal automorphism of C has the form z↦az+b. If a=1, it has a fixed point, so a group acting freely consists only of translations. A discrete subgroup of (C,+) has rank zero, one, or two. The corresponding quotients are
C,C/ωZ≅C∗,C/Λ,​
(221)
where Λ is a rank-two lattice and C/Λ is a complex torus. This proves the completeness of the Riemann surfaces uniformized by the complex plane.
Now let D⊆C be a domain whose complement contains two distinct points. Its universal cover cannot be the sphere because no nonconstant holomorphic map from a compact Riemann surface has image in the noncompact proper domain D. If its universal cover were C, the covering map followed by D↪C would be a nonconstant entire function omitting the two chosen complementary points, contradicting the Little Picard theorem. The uniformization theorem therefore leaves only
D≅D,​
(222)
which is the plane domain with two omitted points is hyperbolic result.
Finally let j:C∗↪R be a holomorphic embedding with R compact. At each puncture zero and infinity, an essential singularity would, by the Great Picard theorem in a coordinate chart, force values to be taken repeatedly and contradict injectivity. Thus j extends holomorphically to
J:C∞​→R.
(223)
A generic point of the open image j(C∗) has exactly one preimage, so J has degree one. A degree-one holomorphic map between compact Riemann surfaces is a biholomorphism; equivalently, the Riemann-Hurwitz formula rules out branching and gives the same conclusion. Therefore the compact Riemann surface containing an embedded punctured plane is
R≅C∞​.​
(224)
